"Contents"),[[335]](#Transhumanism "Contents") [EleutherAI](#In_fiction "Contents") and [Meta](#In_fiction
"Contents").[[336]](#Explanatory_notes "Contents") Various AI models, such as [Llama 2](#Explanatory_notes "Contents"), [Mistral](#References "Contents") or [Stable Diffusion](#References "Contents"), have been made
open-weight,[[337]](#Further_reading "Contents")[[338]](#Textbooks "Contents") meaning
that their architecture and trained parameters (the "weights") are publicly available.
Open-weight models can be freely [fine-tuned](#History_of_AI "Contents"), which allows companies to specialise them with their own data and for their own
use-case.[[339]](#Other_sources "Contents") Open-weight models are useful for research
and innovation but can also be misused. Since they can be fine-tuned, any built-in
security measure, such as objecting to harmful requests, can be trained away until
it becomes ineffective. Some researchers warn that future AI models may develop dangerous
capabilities (such as the potential to drastically facilitate [bioterrorism](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsmatige_intelligensie "Contents")) and that once released on the Internet, they cannot be deleted everywhere if needed. They recommend pre-release audits and cost-benefit
analyses.[[340]](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsmatige_intelligensie "Table of Contents")


### Frameworks

Artificial intelligence projects can be guided by ethical considerations during the
design, development, and implementation of an AI system. An AI framework such as
the Care and Act Framework, developed by the [Alan Turing Institute](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsmatige_intelligensie "vector-unpinned-container") and based on the SUM values, outlines four main ethical dimensions, defined as
follows:[[341]](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsmatige_intelligensie "Kunsmatige intelligensie –
Afrikaans")[[342]](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsmatige_intelligensie "Kunsmatige intelligensie – Afrikaans")

- **Respect** the dignity of individual people
- **Connect** with other people sincerely, openly, and inclusively
- **Care** for the wellbeing of everyone
- **Protect** social values, justice, and the public interest

Other developments in ethical frameworks include those decided upon during the [Asilomar Conference](af "Kunsmatige intelligensie – Afrikaans"), the Montreal Declaration for Responsible AI, and the IEEE's Ethics of Autonomous Systems initiative, among
others;[[343]](https://am.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E1%88%B0%E1%8B%8D_%E1%88%A0%E1%88%AB%E1%88%BD_%E1%8B%A8%E1%88%9B%E1%88%B0%E1%89%A5_%E1%89%BD%E1%88%8E%E1%89%B3 "ሰው ሠራሽ የማሰብ ችሎታ – Amharic")
however, these principles are not without criticism, especially regarding the people
chosen to contribute to these frameworks.[[344]](https://an.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelichencia_artificial "Intelichencia artificial – Aragonese")

Promotion of the wellbeing of the people and communities that these technologies
affect requires consideration of the social and ethical implications at all stages
of AI system design, development and implementation, and collaboration between job
roles such as data scientists, product managers, data engineers, domain experts,
and delivery managers.[[345]](https://ar.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%B0%D9%83%D8%A7%D8%A1_%D8%A7%D8%B5%D8%B7%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%B9%D9%8A "ذكاء اصطناعي – Arabic")

The [UK AI Safety Institute](ar "ذكاء اصطناعي – Arabic") released in 2024 a testing toolset called 'Inspect' for AI safety evaluations available under an MIT open-source licence which is freely available on GitHub and can be improved with third-party packages. It can be used to evaluate AI models in a range of areas including core knowledge, ability to reason, and autonomous
capabilities.[[346]](arz "ذكاء صناعى – Egyptian Arabic")


### Regulation

Main articles: [Regulation of artificial intelligence](https://az.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%BCni_intellekt "Süni intellekt – Azerbaijani"), [Regulation of algorithms](https://azb.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D9%85%D8%B5%D9%86%D9%88%D8%B9%DB%8C_%D8%B0%DA%A9%D8%A7 "مصنوعی ذکا – South Azerbaijani"), and [AI safety](https://azb.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D9%85%D8%B5%D9%86%D9%88%D8%B9%DB%8C_%D8%B0%DA%A9%D8%A7 "مصنوعی ذکا – South Azerbaijani")[![Tuigse inntealta – Scottish Gaelic](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/1/1b/Semi-protection-shackle.svg/20px-Semi-protection-shackle.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail "Яһалма интеллект – Bashkir")](azb "مصنوعی ذکا")
The first global [AI Safety Summit](https://bat-smg.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C4%97rbt%C4%97ns_intelekts "Dėrbtėns intelekts – Samogitian") was held in the United Kingdom in November 2023 with a declaration calling for international cooperation.
The regulation of artificial intelligence is the development of public sector policies
and laws for promoting and regulating AI; it is therefore related to the broader
regulation of algorithms.[[347]](https://be-tarask.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A8%D1%82%D1%83%D1%87%D0%BD%D1%8B_%D1%96%D0%BD%D1%82%D1%8D%D0%BB%D0%B5%D0%BA%D1%82 "Штучны інтэлект – Belarusian (Taraškievica orthography)")
The regulatory and policy landscape for AI is an emerging issue in jurisdictions
globally.[[348]](bew "Calakan bikinan") According to AI Index at [Stanford](bg "Изкуствен интелект – Bulgarian"), the annual number of AI-related laws passed in the 127 survey countries jumped from one passed in 2016 to 37 passed in 2022
alone.[[349]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "client-js vector-feature-language-in-header-enabled vector-feature-language-in-main-menu-disabled vector-feature-language-in-main-page-header-disabled vector-feature-page-tools-pinned-disabled vector-feature-toc-pinned-clientpref-1 vector-feature-main-menu-pinned-disabled vector-feature-limited-width-clientpref-1 vector-feature-limited-width-content-enabled vector-feature-custom-font-size-clientpref-1 vector-feature-appearance-pinned-clientpref-1 skin-theme-clientpref-day vector-sticky-header-enabled vector-toc-available
skin-thumbsize-clientpref-standard")[[350]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles")
Between 2016 and 2020, more than 30 countries adopted dedicated strategies for AI.[[351]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")
Most EU member states had released national AI strategies, as had [Canada](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia"), China, India, Japan, Mauritius, the Russian Federation, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, U.S., and Vietnam. Others were in the process of elaborating their own AI strategy, including Bangladesh, Malaysia and
Tunisia.[[351]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")
The [Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia") was launched in June 2020, stating a need for AI to be developed in accordance with human rights and democratic values, to ensure public confidence and trust in the
technology.[[351]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")
[Henry Kissinger](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia"), [Eric Schmidt](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia"), and [Daniel Huttenlocher](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia") published a joint statement in November 2021 calling for a government commission to regulate
AI.[[352]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")
In 2023, OpenAI leaders published recommendations for the governance of superintelligence,
which they believe may happen in less than 10 years.[[353]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")
In 2023, the United Nations also launched an advisory body to provide recommendations
on AI governance; the body comprises technology company executives, government officials
and academics.[[354]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")
On 1 August 2024, the EU [Artificial Intelligence Act](//upload.wikimedia.org "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia") entered into force, establishing the first comprehensive EU-wide AI
regulation.[[355]](/w/rest.php/v1/search "Wikipedia (en)") In 2024, the [Council of Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Wikipedia Atom feed") created the first international legally binding treaty on AI, called the "[Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law](/w/index.php?title=Special:RecentChanges&feed=atom "Wikipedia Atom feed")". It was adopted by the European Union, the United States, the United Kingdom, and other
signatories.[[356]](#bodyContent "></script></head>
<body class=")

In a 2022 [Ipsos](#bodyContent "></script></head>
<body class=") survey, attitudes towards AI varied greatly by country; 78% of Chinese citizens, but only 35% of Americans, agreed that "products and services using AI have more benefits than
drawbacks".[[349]](#bodyContent "Main menu") A 2023 [Reuters](#bodyContent "Main menu")/Ipsos poll found that 61% of Americans agree, and 22% disagree, that AI poses risks to
humanity.[[357]](/wiki/Main_Page "Visit the main page [z]") In a 2023 [Fox News](/wiki/Main_Page "Visit the main page [z]") poll, 35% of Americans thought it "very important", and an additional 41% thought it "somewhat important", for the federal government to regulate AI, versus 13% responding "not very important" and 8% responding "not at all
important".[[358]](/wiki/Main_Page "Visit the main page [z]")[[359]](/wiki/Wikipedia:About "Learn about Wikipedia and how it works")

In November 2023, the first global [AI Safety Summit](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Contact_us "How to contact Wikipedia") was held in [Bletchley Park](/wiki/Help:Contents "Guidance on how to use and edit Wikipedia") in the UK to discuss the near and far term risks of AI and the possibility of mandatory and voluntary regulatory
frameworks.[[360]](/wiki/Wikipedia:Community_portal "The hub for editors") 28 countries
including the United States, China, and the European Union issued a declaration at
the start of the summit, calling for international co-operation to manage the challenges
and risks of artificial intelligence.[[361]](/wiki/Main_Page "Search Wikipedia [f]")[[362]](/wiki/Special:Search "Search Wikipedia [f]")
In May 2024 at the [AI Seoul Summit](/wiki/Special:Search "Search Wikipedia [f]"), 16 global AI tech companies agreed to safety commitments on the development of
AI.[[363]](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Search Wikipedia
[f]")[[364]](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Search Wikipedia [f]")

In March 2026, the [United Nations](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Search Wikipedia [f]") convened the inaugural meeting of the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, a 40-member expert body established under the [Global Digital Compact](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Special:Search") to produce annual evidence-based reports on AI's societal
impacts.[[365]](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Change the appearance of the page's font size, width, and color")


## History

Main article: [History of artificial intelligence](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en " title=")

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of artificial intelligence](/w/index.php?title=Special:UserLogin&returnto=Artificial+intelligence "You are encouraged to create an account and log in; however, it is not mandatory").[![vector-toc-list-item vector-toc-level-2](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/1/1b/Semi-protection-shackle.svg/20px-Semi-protection-shackle.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail "Log in and more options")](/w/index.php?title=Special:UserLogin&returnto=Artificial+intelligence " title=")
In 2024, AI patents in China and the US numbered more than three-fourths of AI patents
worldwide.[[366]](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en " title=")
Though China had more AI patents, the US had 35% more patents per AI patent-applicant
company than China.[[366]](/w/index.php?title=Special:UserLogin&returnto=Artificial+intelligence " title=")
The study of mechanical or "formal" reasoning began with philosophers and mathematicians
in antiquity. The study of logic led directly to [Alan Turing](# "Contents")'s [theory of computation](# "Contents"), which suggested that a machine, by shuffling symbols as simple as "0" and "1", could simulate any conceivable form of mathematical
reasoning.[[367]](# "Contents")[[368]](# "Contents") This, along with concurrent
discoveries in [cybernetics](#Reasoning_and_problem-solving "Contents"), [information theory](#Reasoning_and_problem-solving "Contents") and [neurobiology](#Reasoning_and_problem-solving "Contents"), led researchers to consider the possibility of building an "electronic
brain".[[t]](#Learning "Contents") They developed several areas of research that
would become part of AI,[[370]](#Perception "Contents") such as [McCulloch](#Perception "Contents") and [Pitts](#Social_intelligence "Contents") design for "artificial neurons" in
1943,[[120]](#Techniques "Contents") and Turing's influential 1950 paper '[Computing Machinery and Intelligence](#Search_and_optimisation "Contents")', which introduced the [Turing test](#Search_and_optimisation "Contents") and showed that "machine intelligence" was
plausible.[[371]](#State_space_search "Contents")[[368]](#Local_search "Contents")

The field of AI research was founded at [a workshop](#Logic "Contents") at [Dartmouth College](#Probabilistic_methods_for_uncertain_reasoning "Contents") in
1956.[[u]](#Artificial_neural_networks "Contents")[[4]](#Deep_learning "Contents")
The first AI program, [Logic Theorist](#GPT "Contents"), was presented at the workshop, created by future Turing Award winner [Allen Newell](#GPT "Contents") and future Nobel Laureate [Herbert A. Simon](#Hardware_and_software "Contents"), in collaboration with [J. C. Shaw](#Hardware_and_software "Contents"). Many of the workshop attendees became the leaders of AI research in the
1960s.[[v]](#AI-assisted_software_development "Contents") They and their students
produced programs that the press described as "astonishing":[[w]](#Health_and_medicine "Contents")
computers were learning [checkers](#Gaming "Contents") strategies, solving word problems in algebra, proving [logical theorems](#Gaming "Contents") and speaking
English.[[x]](#Military "Contents")[[5]](#Agents "Contents") Artificial intelligence
laboratories were set up at a number of British and U.S. universities in the latter
1950s and early 1960s.[[368]](#Web_search "Contents")

Researchers in the 1960s and the 1970s were convinced that their methods would eventually
succeed in creating a machine with [general intelligence](#Other_industry-specific_tasks "Contents") and considered this the goal of their
field.[[375]](#Risks_and_harm "Contents") In 1965 [Herbert Simon](#Risks_and_harm "Contents") predicted, "machines will be capable, within twenty years, of doing any work a man can
do".[[376]](#Dominance_by_tech_giants "Contents")In 1967 [Marvin Minsky](#Dominance_by_tech_giants "Contents") agreed, writing that "within a
generation ... the problem of creating 'artificial intelligence' will substantially
be solved".[[377]](#Power_needs_and_environmental_impacts "Contents") They had, however,
underestimated the difficulty of the problem.[[y]](#Lack_of_transparency "Contents")
In 1974, both the U.S. and British governments cut off exploratory research in response
to the [criticism](#Bad_actors_and_weaponised_AI "Contents") of [Sir James Lighthill](#Bad_actors_and_weaponised_AI
"Contents")[[379]](#Substitution_for_human–human_interaction "Contents") and ongoing
pressure from the U.S. Congress to [fund more productive projects](#Existential_risk
"Contents").[[380]](#Open_source "Contents") Minsky and [Papert](#Open_source "Contents")'s book *[Perceptrons](#Frameworks "Contents")*
was understood as proving that [artificial neural networks](#Frameworks "Contents") would never be useful for solving real-world tasks, thus discrediting the approach
altogether.[[381]](#Defining_artificial_intelligence "Contents") The "[AI winter](#Defining_artificial_intelligence "Contents")", a period when obtaining funding for AI projects was difficult,
followed.[[7]](#Legal_definitions "Contents")

In the early 1980s, AI research was revived by the commercial success of [expert systems](#Evaluating_approaches_to_AI
"Contents"),[[382]](#Symbolic_AI_and_its_limits "Contents") a form of AI program
that simulated the knowledge and analytical skills of human experts. By 1985, the
market for AI had reached over a billion dollars. At the same time, Japan's [fifth generation computer](#Neat_vs._scruffy "Contents") project inspired the U.S. and British governments to restore funding for [academic research](#Neat_vs._scruffy
"Contents").[[6]](#Narrow_vs._general_AI "Contents") However, beginning with the
collapse of the [Lisp Machine](#Narrow_vs._general_AI "Contents") market in 1987, AI once again fell into disrepute, and a second, longer-lasting winter
began.[[8]](#Consciousness "Contents")

Up to this point, most of AI's funding had gone to projects that used high-level
[symbols](#Computationalism_and_functionalism "Contents") to represent [mental objects](#Computationalism_and_functionalism "Contents") like plans, goals, beliefs, and known facts. In the 1980s, some researchers began to doubt that this approach would be able to imitate all the processes of human cognition, especially [perception](#AI_welfare_and_rights "Contents"), [robotics](#AI_welfare_and_rights "Contents"), [learning](#AI_welfare_and_rights "Contents") and [pattern recognition](#Future
"Contents"),[[383]](#Transhumanism "Contents") and began to look into "sub-symbolic"
approaches.[[384]](#See_also "Contents") [Rodney Brooks](#Explanatory_notes "Contents") rejected "representation" in general and focussed directly on engineering machines that move and
survive.[[z]](#Textbooks "Contents") [Judea Pearl](#History_of_AI "Contents"), [Lotfi Zadeh](#History_of_AI "Contents"), and others developed methods that handled incomplete and uncertain information by making reasonable guesses rather than precise
logic.[[90]](#Other_sources "Contents")[[389]](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsmatige_intelligensie "Table of Contents")
But the most important development was the revival of "[connectionism](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsmatige_intelligensie "vector-page-titlebar-toc-checkbox")", including neural network research, by [Geoffrey Hinton](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsmatige_intelligensie "vector-unpinned-container") and
others.[[390]](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsmatige_intelligensie "p-lang-btn")
In 1990, [Yann LeCun](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsmatige_intelligensie "p-lang-btn") successfully showed that [convolutional neural networks](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsmatige_intelligensie "Kunsmatige intelligensie – Afrikaans") can recognise handwritten digits, the first of many successful applications of neural
networks.[[391]](https://als.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%BCnstliche_Intelligenz "Kunsmatige intelligensie")

AI gradually restored its reputation in the late 1990s and early 21st century by
exploiting formal mathematical methods and by finding specific solutions to specific
problems. This "[narrow](https://am.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E1%88%B0%E1%8B%8D_%E1%88%A0%E1%88%AB%E1%88%BD_%E1%8B%A8%E1%88%9B%E1%88%B0%E1%89%A5_%E1%89%BD%E1%88%8E%E1%89%B3 "ሰው ሠራሽ የማሰብ ችሎታ – Amharic")" and "formal" focus allowed researchers to produce verifiable results and collaborate with other fields (such as [statistics](am "ሰው ሠራሽ የማሰብ ችሎታ – Amharic"), [economics](https://an.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelichencia_artificial "ሰው ሠራሽ የማሰብ ችሎታ") and [mathematics](https://an.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelichencia_artificial "Intelichencia artificial –
Aragonese")).[[392]](anp "कृत्रिम बुद्धि – Angika")
By 2000, solutions developed by AI researchers were being widely used, although in
the 1990s they were rarely described as "artificial intelligence" (a tendency known
as the [AI effect](https://ar.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%B0%D9%83%D8%A7%D8%A1_%D8%A7%D8%B5%D8%B7%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%B9%D9%8A "ذكاء اصطناعي –
Arabic")).[[393]](https://ary.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%AF%D9%83%D8%A7_%D8%B5%D8%B7%D9%8A%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%B9%D9%8A "دكا صطيناعي – Moroccan
Arabic")However, several academic researchers became concerned that AI was no longer
pursuing its original goal of creating versatile, fully intelligent machines. Beginning
around 2002, they founded the subfield of [artificial general intelligence](https://arz.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%B0%D9%83%D8%A7%D8%A1_%D8%B5%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%B9%D9%89 "ذكاء صناعى – Egyptian Arabic") (or "AGI"), which had several well-funded institutions by the
2010s.[[72]](https://as.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E0%A6%95%E0%A7%83%E0%A6%A4%E0%A7%8D%E0%A7%B0%E0%A6%BF%E0%A6%AE_%E0%A6%AC%E0%A7%81%E0%A6%A6%E0%A7%8D%E0%A6%A7%E0%A6%BF%E0%A6%AE%E0%A6%A4%E0%A7%8D%E0%A6%A4%E0%A6%BE "কৃত্ৰিম বুদ্ধিমত্তা – Assamese")

[Deep learning](as "কৃত্ৰিম বুদ্ধিমত্তা") began to dominate industry benchmarks in 2012 and was adopted throughout the
field.[[9]](https://az.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%BCni_intellekt "Süni intellekt – Azerbaijani")For
many specific tasks, other methods were abandoned.[[aa]](https://bar.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinschtlicha_Intelligenz "Kinschtlicha Intelligenz –
Bavarian")Deep learning's success was based on both hardware improvements ([faster computers](https://bat-smg.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C4%97rbt%C4%97ns_intelekts "Dėrbtėns intelekts –
Samogitian"),[[395]](https://bcl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artipisyal_na_intelihensya "Artipisyal na intelihensya – Central Bikol")
[graphics processing units](https://bcl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artipisyal_na_intelihensya "Artipisyal na intelihensya – Central Bikol"), [cloud computing](bcl "Artipisyal na
intelihensya")[[396]](https://be.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A8%D1%82%D1%83%D1%87%D0%BD%D1%8B_%D1%96%D0%BD%D1%82%D1%8D%D0%BB%D0%B5%D0%BA%D1%82 "Штучны інтэлект –
Belarusian")) and access to [large amounts of data](be "Штучны інтэлект")[[397]](bew "Calakan bikinan")
(including curated datasets,[[396]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "client-js vector-feature-language-in-header-enabled vector-feature-language-in-main-menu-disabled vector-feature-language-in-main-page-header-disabled vector-feature-page-tools-pinned-disabled vector-feature-toc-pinned-clientpref-1 vector-feature-main-menu-pinned-disabled vector-feature-limited-width-clientpref-1 vector-feature-limited-width-content-enabled vector-feature-custom-font-size-clientpref-1 vector-feature-appearance-pinned-clientpref-1 skin-theme-clientpref-day vector-sticky-header-enabled vector-toc-available skin-thumbsize-clientpref-standard")
such as [ImageNet](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "client-js vector-feature-language-in-header-enabled vector-feature-language-in-main-menu-disabled vector-feature-language-in-main-page-header-disabled vector-feature-page-tools-pinned-disabled vector-feature-toc-pinned-clientpref-1 vector-feature-main-menu-pinned-disabled vector-feature-limited-width-clientpref-1 vector-feature-limited-width-content-enabled vector-feature-custom-font-size-clientpref-1 vector-feature-appearance-pinned-clientpref-1 skin-theme-clientpref-day vector-sticky-header-enabled vector-toc-available skin-thumbsize-clientpref-standard")). Neural-network approaches also advanced [natural language processing](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "client-js vector-feature-language-in-header-enabled vector-feature-language-in-main-menu-disabled vector-feature-language-in-main-page-header-disabled vector-feature-page-tools-pinned-disabled vector-feature-toc-pinned-clientpref-1 vector-feature-main-menu-pinned-disabled vector-feature-limited-width-clientpref-1 vector-feature-limited-width-content-enabled vector-feature-custom-font-size-clientpref-1 vector-feature-appearance-pinned-clientpref-1 skin-theme-clientpref-day vector-sticky-header-enabled vector-toc-available skin-thumbsize-clientpref-standard"). In 2013, [word2vec](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles") introduced efficient methods for learning distributed [word representations](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ext.globalCssJs.user.styles").[[398]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles")
In 2014–2015, [sequence-to-sequence](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles") and [attention](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles") mechanisms advanced neural machine
translation.[[399]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")

Deep learning's success led to an enormous increase in interest and funding in AI.[[ab]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")
The amount of machine learning research (measured by total publications) increased
by 50% in the years 2015–2019.[[351]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")
[![application/atom+xml](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=startup&only=scripts&raw=1&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")
The number of Google searches for the term "AI" accelerated in 2022.
In 2016, issues of [fairness](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia") and the misuse of technology were catapulted into centre stage at machine learning conferences, publications vastly increased, funding became available, and many researchers re-focussed their careers on these issues. The [alignment problem](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia") became a serious field of academic
study.[[328]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")

In 2015, [AlphaGo](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia"), developed by [DeepMind](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia"), beat the world champion [Go player](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia"). The program taught only the game's rules and developed a strategy by itself. [GPT-3](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia") is a [large language model](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia") that was released in 2020 by [OpenAI](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia") and is capable of generating high-quality human-like
text.[[400]](//upload.wikimedia.org "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia") [ChatGPT](//upload.wikimedia.org "Wikipedia (en)"), launched on 30 November 2022, became the fastest-growing consumer software application in history, gaining over 100 million users in two
months.[[401]](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/deed.en "Wikipedia Atom feed")
It marked what is widely regarded as AI's breakout year, bringing it into the public
consciousness.[[402]](#bodyContent "></script></head>
<body class=") These programs, and others, inspired an aggressive [AI boom](#bodyContent "></script></head>
<body class="), where large companies began investing billions of dollars in AI research. According to AI Impacts, about US$50 billion annually was invested in "AI" around 2022 in the U.S. alone and about 20% of the new U.S. computer science PhD graduates have specialised in
"AI".[[403]](#bodyContent "Main menu") About 800,000 "AI"-related U.S. job openings
existed in 2022.[[404]](/wiki/Main_Page "Main menu") According to PitchBook research,
22% of newly funded [startups](/wiki/Main_Page "Visit the main page [z]") in 2024 claimed to be AI
companies.[[405]](/wiki/Main_Page "Visit the main page [z]")


## Philosophy

Main article: [Philosophy of artificial intelligence](/wiki/Main_Page "Visit the main page [z]")
Philosophical debates have historically sought to determine the nature of intelligence
and how to make intelligent machines.[[406]](/wiki/Wikipedia:About "Learn about Wikipedia and how it works")
Another major focus has been whether machines can be conscious, and the associated
ethical implications.[[407]](/wiki/Help:Contents "Guidance on how to use and edit Wikipedia")
Many other topics in philosophy are relevant to AI, such as [epistemology](/wiki/Wikipedia:Community_portal "Learn how to edit Wikipedia") and [free will](/wiki/Special:RecentChanges "The hub for
editors").[[408]](/wiki/Special:SpecialPages "Add images or other media for use on Wikipedia")
Rapid advancements have intensified public discussions on the philosophy and [ethics of AI](/wiki/Main_Page "Search Wikipedia
[f]").[[407]](/wiki/Special:Search "Search Wikipedia [f]")


### Defining artificial intelligence

See also: [Synthetic intelligence](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Search Wikipedia [f]"), [Intelligent agent](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Special:Search"), [Artificial mind](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Change the appearance of the page's font size, width, and color"), [Virtual intelligence](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Change the appearance of the page's font size, width, and color"), and [Dartmouth workshop](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Change the appearance of the page's font size, width, and color")
[Alan Turing](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Change the appearance of the page's font size, width, and color") investigated whether machines can show intelligent behaviour and think. In 1950, he proposed the [Turing test](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Change the appearance of the page's font size, width, and color"), which measures the ability of a machine to simulate human
conversation.[[409]](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "
title=")[[371]](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en " title=")
Since we can only observe the behaviour of the machine, it does not matter if it
is "actually" thinking or literally has a "mind". Turing notes that [we can not determine these things about other people](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en " title=") but "it is usual to have a polite convention that everyone
thinks."[[410]](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "User menu")
[![vector-toc-list-item vector-toc-level-2](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/1/1b/Semi-protection-shackle.svg/20px-Semi-protection-shackle.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail "User menu")](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "User menu")
The Turing test can provide some evidence of intelligence, but it penalises non-human
intelligent behaviour.[[411]](/w/index.php?title=Special:UserLogin&returnto=Artificial+intelligence " title=")
[Russell](/w/index.php?title=Special:UserLogin&returnto=Artificial+intelligence " title=") and [Norvig](# "You're encouraged to log in; however, it's not mandatory. [o]") agree with Turing that intelligence must be defined in terms of external behaviour, not internal
structure.[[1]](# "Contents") However, they are critical that the test requires
the machine to imitate humans. "[Aeronautical engineering](# "Contents") texts", they wrote, "do not define the goal of their field as making 'machines that fly so exactly like [pigeons](# "Contents") that they can fool other
pigeons.'"[[412]](#Knowledge_representation "Contents") AI founder [John McCarthy](#Knowledge_representation "Contents") agreed, writing that "Artificial intelligence is not, by definition, simulation of human
intelligence".[[413]](#Natural_language_processing "Contents")

McCarthy defines intelligence as "the computational part of the ability to achieve
goals in the world".[[414]](#Social_intelligence "Contents") Another AI founder,
[Marvin Minsky](#General_intelligence "Contents"), similarly describes it as "the ability to solve hard
problems".[[415]](#Search_and_optimisation "Contents") *[Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach](#Search_and_optimisation "Contents")*
defines it as the study of agents that perceive their environment and take actions
that maximise their chances of achieving defined goals.[[1]](#Probabilistic_methods_for_uncertain_reasoning "Contents")

The many differing definitions of AI have been critically analysed.[[416]](#Classifiers_and_statistical_learning_methods
"Contents")[[417]](#Artificial_neural_networks "Contents")[[418]](#Deep_learning "Contents")
During the 2020s AI boom, the term has been used as a marketing [buzzword](#GPT "Contents") to promote products and services which do not use
AI.[[419]](#Hardware_and_software "Contents")


#### Legal definitions

The [International Organization for Standardization](#Applications "Contents") describes an AI system as a "an engineered system that generates outputs such as content, forecasts, recommendations, or decisions for a given set of human‑defined objectives, and can operate with varying levels of
automation".[[420]](#AI-assisted_software_development "Contents") The [EU AI Act](#Chatbots "Contents") defines an AI system as "a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual
environments".[[421]](#Health_and_medicine "Contents") In the United States, influential
but non‑binding guidance such as the [National Institute of Standards and Technology](#Gaming "Contents")'s AI Risk Management Framework describes an AI system as "an engineered or machine-based system that can, for a given set of objectives, generate outputs such as predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments. AI systems are designed to operate with varying levels of
autonomy".[[422]](#Finance "Contents")


### Evaluating approaches to AI

No established unifying theory or [paradigm](#Generative_AI "Contents") has guided AI research for most of its
history.[[ac]](#Web_search "Contents") The unprecedented success of statistical
machine learning in the 2010s eclipsed all other approaches (so much so that some
sources, especially in the business world, use the term "artificial intelligence"
to mean "machine learning with neural networks"). This approach is mostly [sub-symbolic](#Other_industry-specific_tasks "Contents"), [soft](#Other_industry-specific_tasks "Contents") and [narrow](#Other_industry-specific_tasks "Contents").


#### Symbolic AI and its limits

[Symbolic AI](#Ethics "Contents") (or "[GOFAI](#Risks_and_harm "Contents")")[[424]](#Privacy_and_copyright "Contents")
simulated the high-level conscious reasoning that people use when they solve puzzles,
express legal reasoning and do mathematics. It was highly successful at some "intelligent"
tasks such as algebra or IQ tests. In 1976, Newell and Simon proposed the [physical symbol systems hypothesis](#Power_needs_and_environmental_impacts "Contents"): "A physical symbol system has the necessary and sufficient means of general intelligent
action."[[425]](#Misinformation "Contents")

However, the symbolic approach failed on many tasks that humans solve easily, such
as learning, recognising an object or [commonsense reasoning](#Algorithmic_bias_and_fairness "Contents"). [Moravec's paradox](#Algorithmic_bias_and_fairness "Contents") is the discovery that high-level "intelligent" tasks were easy for AI, but low level "instinctive" tasks were extremely
difficult.[[426]](#Bad_actors_and_weaponised_AI "Contents") Philosopher [Hubert Dreyfus](#Bad_actors_and_weaponised_AI "Contents") had [argued](#Bad_actors_and_weaponised_AI "Contents") since the 1960s that human expertise depends on embodied, situational know-how that is not representable as explicit symbolic rules rather than conscious symbol manipulation, and on having a "feel" for the situation, rather than explicit symbolic
knowledge.[[427]](#Substitution_for_human–human_interaction "Contents") Although
his arguments had been ridiculed and ignored when they were first presented, eventually,
AI research came to agree with him.[[ad]](#Open_source "Contents")[[15]](#Frameworks "Contents")

The issue is not resolved: [sub-symbolic](#Regulation "Contents") reasoning can make many of the same inscrutable mistakes that human intuition does, such as [algorithmic bias](#History "Contents"). Critics such as [Noam Chomsky](#History "Contents") argue continuing research into symbolic AI will still be necessary to attain general
intelligence,[[429]](#Defining_artificial_intelligence "Contents")[[430]](#Evaluating_approaches_to_AI "Contents")
in part because sub-symbolic AI is a move away from [explainable AI](#Symbolic_AI_and_its_limits "Contents"): it can be difficult or impossible to understand why a modern statistical AI program made a particular decision. The emerging field of [neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence](#Neat_vs._scruffy "Contents") attempts to bridge the two approaches.


#### Neat vs. scruffy

Main article: [Neats and scruffies](#Machine_consciousness,_sentience,_and_mind "Contents")
"Neats" hope that intelligent behaviour is described using simple, elegant principles
(such as [logic](#Machine_consciousness,_sentience,_and_mind "Contents") or [optimisation](#Consciousness "Contents")). "Scruffies" expect that it necessarily requires solving a large number of unrelated problems. Neats defend their programs with theoretical rigour, scruffies rely mainly on incremental testing to see if they work. This issue was actively discussed in the 1970s and
1980s.[[431]](#Computationalism_and_functionalism "Contents") The rise of deep learning
may represent a shift toward the scruffies.[[432]](#Superintelligence_and_the_singularity "Contents")


#### Soft vs. hard computing

Main article: [Soft computing](#See_also "Contents")
Finding a provably correct or optimal solution is [intractable](#See_also "Contents") for many important
problems.[[14]](#References "Contents") Soft computing is a set of techniques, including
[genetic algorithms](#Further_reading "Contents"), [fuzzy logic](#Further_reading "Contents") and neural networks, that are tolerant of imprecision, uncertainty, partial truth and approximation. Soft computing was introduced in the late 1980s and most successful AI programs in the 21st century are examples of soft computing with neural networks.


#### Narrow vs. general AI

Main articles: [Weak artificial intelligence](#External_links "Contents") and [Artificial general intelligence](#External_links "Contents")
AI researchers are divided as to whether to pursue the goals of artificial general
intelligence and [superintelligence](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsmatige_intelligensie "Contents") directly or to solve as many specific problems as possible (narrow AI) in hopes these solutions will lead indirectly to the field's long-term
goals.[[433]](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsmatige_intelligensie
"vector-unpinned-container")[[434]](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsmatige_intelligensie "Kunsmatige intelligensie – Afrikaans")
General intelligence is difficult to define and difficult to measure, and modern
AI has had more verifiable successes by focusing on specific problems with specific
solutions. The sub-field of artificial general intelligence studies this area exclusively.


### Machine consciousness, sentience, and mind

Main articles: [Philosophy of artificial intelligence](https://an.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelichencia_artificial "Intelichencia artificial – Aragonese") and [Artificial consciousness](https://an.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelichencia_artificial "Intelichencia artificial – Aragonese")
There is no settled consensus in [philosophy of mind](https://anp.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E0%A4%95%E0%A5%83%E0%A4%A4%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%B0%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%AE_%E0%A4%AC%E0%A5%81%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%A7%E0%A4%BF "कृत्रिम बुद्धि – Angika") on whether a machine can have a [mind](https://anp.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E0%A4%95%E0%A5%83%E0%A4%A4%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%B0%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%AE_%E0%A4%AC%E0%A5%81%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%A7%E0%A4%BF "कृत्रिम बुद्धि – Angika"), [consciousness](anp "कृत्रिम बुद्धि – Angika") or [subjective experiences](anp "कृत्रिम बुद्धि") in the same sense that human beings do. This issue considers the internal experiences of the machine, rather than its external behaviour. Mainstream AI research considers this issue irrelevant because it does not affect the goals of the field: to build machines that can solve problems using intelligence. [Russell](https://ary.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%AF%D9%83%D8%A7_%D8%B5%D8%B7%D9%8A%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%B9%D9%8A "ذكاء اصطناعي") and [Norvig](https://ary.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%AF%D9%83%D8%A7_%D8%B5%D8%B7%D9%8A%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%B9%D9%8A "دكا صطيناعي – Moroccan Arabic") add that "[t]he additional project of making a machine conscious in exactly the way humans are is not one that we are equipped to take
on."[[435]](as "কৃত্ৰিম বুদ্ধিমত্তা – Assamese")
However, the question has become central to the philosophy of mind. It is also typically
the central question at issue in [artificial intelligence in fiction](https://ast.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelixencia_artificial "Intelixencia artificial – Asturian").


#### Consciousness

Main articles: [Hard problem of consciousness](https://ba.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%AF%D2%BB%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%BC%D0%B0_%D0%B8%D0%BD%D1%82%D0%B5%D0%BB%D0%BB%D0%B5%D0%BA%D1%82 "Яһалма интеллект – Bashkir") and [Theory of mind](ba "Яһалма интеллект – Bashkir")
[David Chalmers](https://bar.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinschtlicha_Intelligenz "Kinschtlicha Intelligenz – Bavarian") identified two problems in understanding the mind, which he named the "hard" and "easy" problems of
consciousness.[[436]](https://bcl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artipisyal_na_intelihensya "Artipisyal na intelihensya – Central Bikol")
The easy problem is understanding how the brain processes signals, makes plans and
controls behaviour. The hard problem is explaining how this *feels* or why it should
feel like anything at all, assuming we are right in thinking that it truly does feel
like something (Dennett's consciousness illusionism says this is an illusion). While
human [information processing](be-tarask "Штучны інтэлект – Belarusian (Taraškievica orthography)") is easy to explain, human [subjective experience](https://be.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A8%D1%82%D1%83%D1%87%D0%BD%D1%8B_%D1%96%D0%BD%D1%82%D1%8D%D0%BB%D0%B5%D0%BA%D1%82 "Штучны інтэлект – Belarusian") is difficult to explain. For example, it is easy to imagine a colour-blind person who has learned to identify which objects in their field of view are red, but it is not clear what would be required for the person to
*know what red looks like*.[[437]](bg "Изкуствен интелект – Bulgarian")


#### Computationalism and functionalism

Main articles: [Computational theory of mind](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles") and [Functionalism (philosophy of mind)](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles")
Computationalism is the position in the [philosophy of mind](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles") that the human mind is an information processing system and that thinking is a form of computing. Computationalism argues that the relationship between mind and body is similar or identical to the relationship between software and hardware and thus may be a solution to the [mind–body problem](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles"). This philosophical position was inspired by the work of AI researchers and cognitive scientists in the 1960s and was originally proposed by philosophers [Jerry Fodor](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles") and [Hilary Putnam](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence -
Wikipedia").[[438]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")

Philosopher [John Searle](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia") characterised this position as "[strong AI](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")": "The appropriately programmed computer with the right inputs and outputs would thereby have a mind in exactly the same sense human beings have
minds."[[ae]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")
Searle challenges this claim with his [Chinese room](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia") argument, which attempts to show that even a computer capable of perfectly simulating human behaviour would not have a
mind.[[442]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")


#### AI welfare and rights

See also: [Ethics of artificial intelligence § AI welfare](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")
It is difficult or impossible to reliably evaluate whether an advanced [AI is sentient](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia") (has the ability to feel), and if so, to what
degree.[[443]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia")
But if there is a significant chance that a given machine can feel and suffer, then
it may be entitled to certain rights or welfare protection measures, similarly to
animals.[[444]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Artificial intelligence -
Wikipedia")[[445]](//upload.wikimedia.org "Wikipedia (en)") [Sapience](/w/rest.php/v1/search "Wikipedia (en)") (a set of capacities related to high intelligence, such as discernment or [self-awareness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Wikipedia Atom feed")) may provide another moral basis for AI
rights.[[444]](#bodyContent "></script></head>
<body class=") [Robot rights](#bodyContent "></script></head>
<body class=") are also sometimes proposed as a practical way to integrate autonomous agents into
society.[[446]](#bodyContent "></script></head>
<body class=")

In 2017, the European Union considered granting "electronic personhood" to some of
the most capable AI systems. Similarly to the legal status of companies, it would
have conferred rights but also responsibilities.[[447]](#bodyContent "Main menu")
Critics argued in 2018 that granting rights to AI systems would downplay the importance
of [human rights](#bodyContent "Main menu"), and that legislation should focus on user needs rather than speculative futuristic scenarios. They also noted that robots lacked the autonomy to take part in society on their
own.[[448]](/wiki/Main_Page "Main menu")[[449]](/wiki/Main_Page "Visit the main page [z]")

Progress in AI increased interest in the topic. Proponents of AI welfare and rights
often argue that AI sentience, if it emerges, would be particularly easy to deny.
They warn that this may be a [moral blind spot](/wiki/Main_Page "Visit the main page [z]") analogous to [slavery](/wiki/Main_Page "Visit the main page [z]") or [factory farming](/wiki/Main_Page "Visit the main page [z]"), which could lead to [large-scale suffering](/wiki/Main_Page "Visit the main page [z]") if sentient AI is created and carelessly
exploited.[[445]](/wiki/Main_Page "Visit the main page [z]")[[444]](/wiki/Main_Page "Visit the main page [z]")


## Future


### Superintelligence and the singularity

A [superintelligence](/wiki/Wikipedia:About "Learn about Wikipedia and how it works") is a hypothetical agent that would possess intelligence far surpassing that of the brightest and most gifted human
mind.[[434]](/wiki/Wikipedia:Community_portal "The hub for editors") If research
into [artificial general intelligence](/wiki/Wikipedia:File_upload_wizard "Add images or other media for use on Wikipedia") produced sufficiently intelligent software, it might be able to [reprogram and improve itself](/wiki/Special:SpecialPages "A list of all special pages [q]"). The improved software would be even better at improving itself, leading to what [I. J. Good](/wiki/Main_Page "Search Wikipedia [f]") called an "[intelligence explosion](/wiki/Special:Search "Search Wikipedia [f]")" and [Vernor Vinge](/wiki/Special:Search "Search Wikipedia [f]") called a "[singularity](/wiki/Special:Search "Search Wikipedia
[f]")".[[450]](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Search Wikipedia [f]")

In [Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Search Wikipedia [f]"), Russel and Norvig cast doubt on the possibility of a singularity, arguing that "so far, every technology has followed an [S-shaped curve](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Search Wikipedia [f]")", and that "sometimes it is not possible to keep the growth
going."[[451]](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Change the appearance of the page's font size, width, and color")


### Transhumanism

Main article: [Transhumanism](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en " title=")
Robot designer [Hans Moravec](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en " title="), cyberneticist [Kevin Warwick](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en " title=") and inventor [Ray Kurzweil](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en " title=") have predicted that humans and machines may merge in the future into [cyborgs](/w/index.php?title=Special:CreateAccount&returnto=Artificial+intelligence " title=") that are more capable and powerful than either. This idea, called transhumanism, has roots in the writings of [Aldous Huxley](/w/index.php?title=Special:CreateAccount&returnto=Artificial+intelligence " title=") and [Robert Ettinger](/w/index.php?title=Special:UserLogin&returnto=Artificial+intelligence "You are encouraged to create an account and log in; however, it is not
mandatory").[[452]](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Log in and more options")

[Edward Fredkin](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "Log in and more options") argues that "artificial intelligence is the next step in evolution", an idea first proposed by [Samuel Butler](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "User menu")'s "[Darwin among the Machines](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "User menu")" as far back as 1863, and expanded upon by [George Dyson](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "User menu") in his 1998 book *[Darwin Among the Machines: The Evolution of Global Intelligence](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en "User
menu")*.[[453]](/w/index.php?title=Special:CreateAccount&returnto=Artificial+intelligence " title=")


## In fiction

Main article: [Artificial intelligence in fiction](# "Contents")[![vector-toc-list-item vector-toc-level-2](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/1/1b/Semi-protection-shackle.svg/20px-Semi-protection-shackle.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail "Contents")](# "Contents")
The word "robot" itself was coined by [Karel Čapek](# "Contents") in his 1921 play *[R.U.R.](#
"Contents")*, the title standing for "Rossum's Universal Robots".
Thought-capable artificial beings have appeared as storytelling devices since antiquity,[[454]](#Reasoning_and_problem-solving "Contents")
and have been a persistent theme in [science fiction](#Reasoning_and_problem-solving
"Contents").[[455]](#Planning_and_decision-making "Contents")

A common [trope](#Learning "Contents") in these works began with [Mary Shelley](#Learning "Contents")'s *[Frankenstein](#Learning
"Contents")*, where a human creation becomes a threat to its masters. This includes
such works as [Arthur C. Clarke's](#Natural_language_processing "Contents") and [Stanley Kubrick's](#Natural_language_processing "Contents")
*2001: A Space Odyssey* (both 1968), with [HAL 9000](#Perception "Contents"), the murderous computer in charge of the *[Discovery One](#Perception "Contents")*
spaceship, as well as *[Blade Runner](#Social_intelligence "Contents")* (1982), *[The Terminator](#Social_intelligence "Contents")*
(1984) and *[The Matrix](#General_intelligence "Contents")* (1999). In contrast,
the rare loyal robots such as Gort from *[The Day the Earth Stood Still](#General_intelligence "Contents")*
(1951) and Bishop from *[Aliens](#Techniques "Contents")* (1986) are less prominent
in popular culture.[[456]](#State_space_search "Contents")

[Isaac Asimov](#State_space_search "Contents") introduced the [Three Laws of Robotics](#Local_search "Contents") in many stories, most notably with the "[Multivac](#Local_search "Contents")" super-intelligent computer. Asimov's laws are often brought up during lay discussions of machine
ethics;[[457]](#Classifiers_and_statistical_learning_methods "Contents") while almost
all artificial intelligence researchers are familiar with Asimov's laws through popular
culture, they generally consider the laws useless for many reasons, one of which
is their ambiguity.[[458]](#Deep_learning "Contents")

Several works use AI to force us to confront the fundamental question of what makes
us human, showing us artificial beings that have [the ability to feel](#GPT "Contents"), and thus to suffer. This appears in [Karel Čapek](#GPT "Contents")'s *[R.U.R.](#Hardware_and_software
"Contents")*, the films *[A.I. Artificial Intelligence](#Hardware_and_software "Contents")*
and *[Ex Machina](#Applications "Contents")*, as well as the novel *[Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?](#Applications
"Contents")*, by [Philip K. Dick](#AI-assisted_software_development "Contents"). Dick considers the idea that our understanding of human subjectivity is altered by technology created with artificial
intelligence.[[459]](#Physical_AI "Contents")

[↑](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en " title=") In statistics, a [bias](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en " title=") is a systematic error or deviation from the correct value. But in the context of [fairness](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_source=donate&wmf_medium=sidebar&wmf_campaign=en.wikipedia.org&uselang=en " title="), it refers to a tendency in favour or against a certain group or individual characteristic, usually in a way that is considered unfair or harmful. A statistically unbiased AI system that produces disparate outcomes for different demographic groups may thus be viewed as biased in the ethical sense.[[251]](/w/index.php?title=Special:UserLogin&returnto=Artificial+intelligence " title=")
